```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Synthetic teaching participants; no real patient records.
set.seed(6301)
n <- 80
trial <- data.frame(id = sprintf("P%03d", seq_len(n)),
  arm = factor(rep(c("Control", "Treatment"), each = n / 2)),
  age = round(rnorm(n, 60, 9)), sbp_0 = rnorm(n, 145, 12))
trial$sbp_12 <- 25 + .8 * trial$sbp_0 + .1 * (trial$age - 60) -
  7 * (trial$arm == "Treatment") + rnorm(n, 0, 7)
trial$response <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-.5 + .8 * (trial$arm == "Treatment") -
                                     .025 * (trial$sbp_0 - 145)))
trial$sbp_0[c(5, 29, 61)] <- NA_real_
```

## The statistical computing sequence {.smaller}

| Session | Focus |
|---|---|
| 14 | Known-truth simulation: design, performance, failures, and Monte Carlo uncertainty |
| 15 | Bootstrap, permutation, and resampling design |
| 16 | Models, cross-validation, broader tools, course recap, and handoff |

## Learning goals {.smaller}

- Define the analysis sample and inspect a fitted model.
- Extract estimates and predict on new data.
- Distinguish diagnostics from held-out predictive evaluation.
- Fit preprocessing within each training fold and check predictions.
- Connect the tools from Sessions 0–15 in a complete project.
- Deliver results with traceable inputs, code, and environment.

## Session outline {.smaller}

| Block | Content |
|---|---|
| 1 | Analysis sample, formulas, and fitted objects |
| 2 | Prediction and diagnostics |
| 3 | Training folds, preprocessing, and held-out prediction |
| 4 | Leakage, benchmarks, and validation design |
| 5 | Broader computing tools |
| 6 | Course recap and complete project workflow |
| 7 | Reproducible handoff |

Optional binary prediction, numerical methods, and structured text are in the
[supplement](supplement.qmd).

# 1 · Fit and inspect a model {.section-divider}

## Define the target before fitting {.smaller}

| Task | Target | Computing evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Adjusted mean comparison | Model coefficient for treatment at specified covariates | Formula, sample, contrast, interval |
| Predict 12-week SBP | Outcome for a new participant | Predictor availability and held-out error |

These tasks can use similar functions while answering different questions.

## Make the analysis population explicit {.smaller}

```{r}
vars <- c("id", "arm", "sbp_0", "age", "sbp_12")
keep <- complete.cases(trial[, vars])
analysis <- trial[keep, vars]
c(available = nrow(trial), analysed = nrow(analysis), excluded = sum(!keep))
trial$id[!keep]
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(analysis$id))
```

Complete-case filtering is explicit here for teaching. It changes the population
being analysed and may introduce bias; it is not a universal missing-data strategy.

## Read a model formula {.smaller}

```{r}
f <- sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm
f
```

The response is left of `~`; the terms on the right specify predictors.
An intercept is included by default. In formulas, `+` adds model terms rather
than adding the columns numerically.

Use `data = analysis` so the intended source of variables is clear.

## Factors determine the comparison {.smaller}

```{r}
analysis$arm <- factor(analysis$arm, levels = c("Control", "Treatment"))
levels(analysis$arm)
contrasts(analysis$arm)
```

With the treatment contrasts used here, Control is the reference.
`armTreatment` represents the Treatment-versus-Control coefficient conditional
on the other terms in this additive model.

Changing the reference changes coefficient interpretation, not the fitted values.

## Inspect the design matrix {.smaller}

```{r}
X <- model.matrix(f, data = analysis)
head(X, 4)
c(rows = nrow(X), columns = ncol(X), rank = qr(X)$rank)
```

Factors become numeric contrast columns. Collinear columns can make coefficients
unidentifiable even when the formula looks reasonable.

## Fit and inspect the object {.smaller}

```{r}
fit <- lm(f, data = analysis, na.action = na.fail)
class(fit)
c(n = nobs(fit), residual_df = df.residual(fit))
coef(fit)
```

`fit` is a structured R object, not the printed coefficient table.
`na.fail` prevents the model from silently dropping additional rows after we
have defined the analysis sample.

## Extract results with model methods {.smaller}

```{r}
coef(summary(fit))
```

| Function | Result |
|---|---|
| `coef(fit)` | Coefficient estimates |
| `confint(fit)` | Model-based coefficient intervals |
| `fitted(fit)` / `residuals(fit)` | Fitted values / residuals |
| `model.frame(fit)` | Variables and rows used for fitting |

Prefer documented methods to copying numbers out of Console output.

## Build a result table {.smaller}

```{r}
ci <- confint(fit)
results <- data.frame(term = names(coef(fit)),
  estimate = unname(coef(fit)), lower = ci[, 1], upper = ci[, 2],
  row.names = NULL)
results
```

State the outcome's units, reference category, sample size, and adjustment terms.
An adjusted coefficient is not automatically a causal effect.

## Verify rows and fitted values {.smaller}

```{r}
stopifnot(nobs(fit) == nrow(analysis),
  nrow(model.frame(fit)) == nrow(analysis),
  isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(X %*% coef(fit)), as.numeric(fitted(fit)))))
```

This independently checks the link between the matrix, coefficients, and fitted
values. It does not establish that the model assumptions are appropriate.

## Practice: a silent sample change {.smaller}

A report says “80 participants.” The fitted object reports 77 observations.
The analyst used the default missing-value handling in `lm()`.

Which variables and identifiers should be checked? Which denominator belongs
beside the reported coefficient table?

## Practice: inspect the fitted sample {.smaller}

Compare the required variables, the complete-case indicator, `nobs(fit)`, and
`model.frame(fit)`. Record the excluded IDs and the missing fields.

Report the sample actually used by the model. For comparisons between models,
also check whether different formulas cause different rows to be included.

# 2 · Prediction and diagnostics {.section-divider}

## Construct prediction data deliberately {.smaller}

```{r}
new_people <- data.frame(sbp_0 = c(140, 155), age = c(55, 65),
  arm = factor(c("Control", "Treatment"), levels = levels(analysis$arm)))
predict(fit, newdata = new_people)
```

Match predictor names, units, and factor levels. Do not substitute `fitted(fit)`
for predictions on new rows; fitted values describe the training observations.

## Mean-response and prediction intervals {.smaller}

```{r}
mean_ci <- predict(fit, new_people, interval = "confidence")
person_pi <- predict(fit, new_people, interval = "prediction")
round(cbind(mean_ci, prediction_lower = person_pi[, "lwr"],
                     prediction_upper = person_pi[, "upr"]), 2)
```

The confidence interval concerns the conditional **mean** response.
The prediction interval concerns an **individual** future response and also
includes residual variation. Both depend on the model's assumptions.

## Unsupported predictions {.smaller}

- A new factor level may prevent prediction.
- Extrapolation can return a number even far outside the training data.
- A response-derived predictor may be unavailable at deployment.
- A narrow model-based interval does not measure every source of uncertainty.

```{r}
range(analysis$sbp_0)
range(new_people$sbp_0)
```

Inspect prediction inputs before interpreting outputs.

## Residuals versus fitted values {.smaller}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3.8
plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit), pch = 19, col = "#8a7448",
     xlab = "Fitted 12-week SBP", ylab = "Residual (mmHg)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey40")
```

Look for curvature, changing spread, and unusual observations. A pattern suggests
follow-up questions; absence of a visible pattern is not proof of adequacy.

## Preserve identifiers in diagnostics {.smaller}

```{r}
diagnostics <- data.frame(id = analysis$id, fitted = fitted(fit),
  residual = residuals(fit), cook = cooks.distance(fit))
head(diagnostics[order(diagnostics$cook, decreasing = TRUE), ], 3)
```

Row numbers can change after filtering or sorting. An ID makes a diagnostic
traceable to its original record.

## Diagnostics and validation differ {.smaller}

| Evidence | Question |
|---|---|
| Residual plots and influence | Where might the fitted model be inadequate or sensitive? |
| Cross-validation in the next block | How well does the fitting procedure predict held-out observations? |
| External evaluation | Does performance transfer to the target setting? |

Good training fit is not a substitute for held-out evaluation.

# 3 · Held-out prediction {.section-divider}

## Five-fold cross-validation in words {.smaller}

1. Divide the participants into five non-overlapping groups called folds.
2. Fit on four folds and predict the remaining fold.
3. Repeat until every fold has served as the assessment group once.
4. Compare each held-out prediction with its observed outcome.

Each participant receives one prediction from a model trained without that
participant. Pool these prediction errors to estimate performance on new people.

The five fits share training data. Fold scores are not five independent studies.

## The prediction target {.smaller}

Predict 12-week SBP for a new participant from baseline variables.
Assessment outcomes are reserved for scoring after predictions are fixed.

The coefficient table used 77 complete cases. For prediction, return to all
80 participants and learn an imputation rule within each training fold.
These workflows use different samples and missing-data rules. Label both.

## Five folds stratified by arm {.smaller}

```{r}
make_folds <- function(arm, k = 5L) {
  stopifnot(!anyNA(arm), length(k) == 1L, k >= 2L,
            k == as.integer(k), all(table(arm) >= k))
  fold <- integer(length(arm))
  for (i in split(seq_along(arm), arm))
    fold[i] <- sample(rep(seq_len(k), length.out = length(i)))
  fold
}
```

Each participant appears in one assessment fold and four training folds.
Stratification balances arm composition; it does not remove dependence.

## Inspect folds before fitting {.smaller}

```{r}
cv_data <- trial[, c("id", "arm", "age", "sbp_0", "sbp_12")]
set.seed(1651)
fold <- make_folds(cv_data$arm)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(cv_data$id), length(fold) == nrow(cv_data),
          setequal(unique(fold), 1:5), sum(is.na(cv_data$sbp_0)) == 3L)
for (k in 1:5)
  stopifnot(length(intersect(cv_data$id[fold == k],
                            cv_data$id[fold != k])) == 0L)
table(fold, cv_data$arm)
```

Keep IDs with rows so that disjointness can be checked directly.

## One split: learn preprocessing from training rows {.smaller}

```{r}
train <- cv_data[fold != 1, ]
assess <- cv_data[fold == 1, ]
replacement <- mean(train$sbp_0, na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(is.finite(replacement))
train$sbp_0[is.na(train$sbp_0)] <- replacement
assess$sbp_0[is.na(assess$sbp_0)] <- replacement
fold_fit <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm,
               data = train, na.action = na.fail)
head(predict(fold_fit, newdata = assess), 3)
```

The same training mean fills missing values in training and assessment rows.
Mean imputation illustrates information flow; it is not a general missing-data solution.

## One prediction per participant {.smaller}

Preallocate missing predictions and an assessment counter. Each fold fits its own model.

```r
pred <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))
seen <- integer(nrow(data))
for (k in sort(unique(fold))) {
  test <- fold == k
  # Learn preprocessing and fit using data[!test, ].
  # Predict data[test, ] and write into pred[test].
  seen[test] <- seen[test] + 1L
}
```

Check that every counter is one and every prediction is finite.

## A reusable prediction function {.smaller}

The lab supplies the scaffold. These lines belong **inside** its fold loop:

```r
train <- data[!test, ]; assess <- data[test, ]
m <- mean(train$sbp_0, na.rm = TRUE)
if (!is.finite(m)) stop("training baseline entirely missing")
train$sbp_0[is.na(train$sbp_0)] <- m
assess$sbp_0[is.na(assess$sbp_0)] <- m
fold_fit <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm,
               data = train, na.action = na.fail)
pred[test] <- predict(fold_fit, newdata = assess)
```

The function returns predictions in the original participant order.

```{r}
#| include: false
cv_predict <- function(data, fold) {
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(data$id), length(fold) == nrow(data),
            !anyNA(fold), length(unique(fold)) >= 2L)
  pred <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))
  seen <- integer(nrow(data))
  for (k in sort(unique(fold))) {
    test <- fold == k
    train <- data[!test, ]; assess <- data[test, ]
    stopifnot(!any(train$id %in% assess$id))
    m <- mean(train$sbp_0, na.rm = TRUE)
    if (!is.finite(m)) stop("training baseline entirely missing")
    train$sbp_0[is.na(train$sbp_0)] <- m
    assess$sbp_0[is.na(assess$sbp_0)] <- m
    fold_fit <- lm(sbp_12 ~ sbp_0 + age + arm,
                   data = train, na.action = na.fail)
    pred[test] <- predict(fold_fit, newdata = assess)
    seen[test] <- seen[test] + 1L
  }
  stopifnot(all(seen == 1L), all(is.finite(pred)))
  pred
}
```

## Score predictions against a simple benchmark {.smaller}

```{r}
held_out <- cv_predict(cv_data, fold)
benchmark <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(cv_data))
for (k in sort(unique(fold)))
  benchmark[fold == k] <- mean(cv_data$sbp_12[fold != k])
rmse <- function(observed, predicted) {
  stopifnot(length(observed) == length(predicted),
            all(is.finite(observed)), all(is.finite(predicted)))
  sqrt(mean((observed - predicted)^2))
}
scores <- c(model = rmse(cv_data$sbp_12, held_out),
            benchmark = rmse(cv_data$sbp_12, benchmark))
scores
```

Pool participant squared errors before taking the square root.
Use identical folds for the model and the training-mean benchmark.

# 4 · Leakage and validation design {.section-divider}

## A deliberately leaky comparison {.smaller}

```{r}
leaky <- cv_data
leaky$sbp_0[is.na(leaky$sbp_0)] <- mean(leaky$sbp_0, na.rm = TRUE)
c(valid = scores[["model"]],
  leaky = rmse(cv_data$sbp_12, cv_predict(leaky, fold)))
```

Global imputation lets assessment covariates influence the learned rule.
Leakage need not improve the score in a particular sample. Audit information flow.

## Diagnose leakage before comparing scores {.smaller}

| Step | Valid location |
|---|---|
| Fixed, prespecified unit conversion | Can be applied to all rows |
| Mean imputation or scaling estimated from data | Training fold |
| Choose features using outcome associations | Training fold, with selection validated |
| Select a model or tuning parameter | Inner validation, separate from final evaluation |
| Compute RMSE | Held-out outcomes after predictions are fixed |

A fixed rule is different from a rule estimated using assessment data.

## Grouped and temporal validation {.smaller}

| Deployment question | Appropriate split idea |
|---|---|
| Predict a new participant | Keep all visits of a participant together |
| Predict at a new clinic | Hold out clinics |
| Predict future outcomes | Train on earlier observations; assess later observations |

Random row folds answer the wrong question if the same participant appears on both sides.

## Selection and final evaluation {.smaller}

Trying many models and reporting the lowest CV error uses the evaluation data
to make a selection. The selected score can be optimistic.

Use a prespecified candidate, an untouched test set, or nested cross-validation:

1. An outer split reserves data for evaluation.
2. Inner training splits choose features and tuning parameters.
3. Refit the selected procedure on outer training data; predict outer assessment data.

After evaluation, a final model can be fitted to the intended full training set.

## Practice: find the information leak {.smaller}

A student fills missing baseline values using all participants, chooses the
best of 20 formulas by CV, and reports that formula's minimum CV error.

Which steps used assessment information? Where should preprocessing happen?
What evaluation data remain available after selecting the formula?

## Practice: a valid evaluation plan {.smaller}

- Estimate preprocessing within training data.
- Prespecify the model for today's exercise.
- For model selection, reserve untouched evaluation data or use nested CV.
- For repeated visits, keep each participant entirely on one side of a split.
- Repeating folds measures split sensitivity, not independent sampling uncertainty.

# 5 · Choosing computing tools {.section-divider}

## The question determines the tool {.smaller}

| Project need | Starting point | What to check |
|---|---|---|
| Estimate an adjusted mean difference | `lm()` | Sample, coding, assumptions, interval |
| Model a binary outcome | `glm(..., family = binomial)` | Outcome coding, probability scale, calibration |
| Quantify uncertainty in a statistic | Bootstrap | Resampling unit and stable estimates |
| Test a randomization null | Permutation | Allowed assignments and null definition |
| Evaluate prediction on new people | Cross-validation | Training-only fitting and relevant splits |

Use the simplest method that answers the question and whose assumptions you
can explain. Complex software does not remove the need to check its inputs.

## Beyond model fitting: numerical computing {.smaller}

| Need | R tool | Verification |
|---|---|---|
| Find a value where a function is zero | `uniroot()` | Check the function is near zero at the answer |
| Minimize an objective | `optim()` | Inspect convergence and compare starting values |
| Compute an area under a curve | `integrate()` | Inspect numerical error and compare a known case |

For example, an estimated parameter may minimize an error function. A returned
number alone does not establish convergence, uniqueness, or scientific validity.

Worked code is available in the [optional supplement](supplement.qmd).

## A project also depends on its data interface {.smaller}

- Preserve participant IDs when importing, joining, filtering, and predicting.
- Validate units, factor levels, dates, missing values, and expected row counts.
- Turn repeated calculations into functions with explicit inputs and outputs.
- Record warnings and failures instead of silently removing inconvenient rows.

R and Python can implement the same workflow. Choose tools your team can review
and rerun. Validate AI-generated code using the same checks as code you write.

## One project connects the sessions {.smaller}

**Example:** analyse a two-arm study with baseline and follow-up SBP.

1. Define the scientific question, outcome, comparison, and analysis unit.
2. Import data, check IDs and units, join visits, and describe missingness.
3. Plot the data and implement the analysis in checked functions.
4. Fit a model or choose a resampling method that matches the question.
5. Interpret the result with uncertainty and limitations.
6. Render a report and package the code, inputs, and environment for review.

Git records the changes. A clean rerun checks that the report follows from the code.

## Different questions require different evidence {.smaller}

| Question about the study | Relevant evidence |
|---|---|
| How large is the mean difference? | Estimate in mmHg with an interval |
| Is the result inconsistent with the randomization null? | A justified test and p-value |
| Can we predict a new patient's SBP? | Held-out error against a benchmark |
| Does the method work under assumed conditions? | Simulation with known truth |
| Can another analyst reproduce the result? | Inputs, code, versions, checks, and rerun instructions |

A small p-value does not establish accurate prediction. A reproducible report
can still contain a poorly chosen analysis. Each claim needs the right evidence.

## Capstone review: what would you check? {.smaller}

A report joins visits by row position, drops missing values silently, trains
and evaluates a model on the same people, and pastes results into slides by hand.

Identify a correction using each part of the course:

- Data structure and joins.
- Analysis sample and validation.
- Reusable code and checks.
- Reproducible reporting and version control.

Explain what evidence would convince a colleague that each correction worked.

# 7 · Reproducible handoff {.section-divider}

## Record both analysis workflows {.smaller}

```{r}
predictions <- data.frame(id = cv_data$id, fold = fold,
  observed = cv_data$sbp_12, prediction = held_out, benchmark = benchmark)
analysis_bundle <- list(formula = formula(fit),
  analysed_ids = analysis$id, excluded_ids = trial$id[!keep],
  coefficients = results, predictions = predictions, rmse = scores,
  input_seed = 6301, fold_seed = 1651, rng = RNGkind(),
  missing_policy = "Complete-case descriptive fit; training-fold mean imputation for CV",
  session = sessionInfo())
```

Document the input and code revision with the saved results.

## Save inspectable outputs {.smaller}

```r
dir.create("output", showWarnings = FALSE)
saveRDS(analysis_bundle, "output/analysis-bundle.rds")
write.csv(results, "output/coefficients.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(predictions, "output/held-out-predictions.csv", row.names = FALSE)
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), "output/session-info.txt")
```

Read the bundle back and check its IDs, coefficients, and predictions.
The lab also saves RMSE and a README with the rerun instructions.

## Package versions are part of the environment {.smaller}

`sessionInfo()` records the active R session but does not recreate its packages.
`renv` adds a project library and a lockfile describing package dependencies.

```r
# Optional: run interactively in a dedicated project, outside report rendering.
renv::init()
renv::snapshot()
# In a clone with the committed lockfile:
renv::restore()
```

These setup commands are optional. A lockfile records dependencies, while the
README documents data access, the R version, and system requirements.

## A reproducible delivery check {.smaller}

1. Open a clean R session in the documented project environment.
2. Obtain the specified input and run the analysis from the documented entry point.
3. Confirm sample counts, key uniqueness, coefficient names, and prediction checks.
4. Render the report and inspect tables and figures.
5. Confirm that the outputs identify their input, code, and environment versions.

Use a colleague's rerun to test the instructions, not only your current workspace.

## Lab route and exit check {.smaller}

Fit and inspect a model; predict new rows; complete the checked CV scaffold;
compare with a benchmark; diagnose leakage; review the course workflow;
save a reproducible handoff.

**Explain:** Why are there 77 rows in the coefficient analysis and 80 held-out
predictions? Which rows learned each imputation value? How does an ID stay
attached to its prediction?

## Summary {.smaller}

Define the sample, inspect the model, and label predictions. Fit preprocessing
inside training folds, check held-out predictions, and retain the evidence
needed to reproduce the result.
